name: delegate_to_agent
description: Hand off a self-contained sub-task to a separate local AI agent that runs in its own session. ASYNCHRONOUS: returns a task_id right away and the sub-agent keeps working in the background — this call never blocks. So you can fan out several delegations at once and keep working, then collect the results with get_delegation_status by passing the task_ids array (one id to poll a single task, or many at once to poll the whole fan-out in one call) — or stop one early with cancel_delegation(task_id). The sub-agent CANNOT see this conversation, your open files, or earlier turns — it starts cold, so `task` must carry everything it needs. Best for independent, parallelizable work you can describe up front; not for steps that need your ongoing back-and-forth. RECOGNIZING AN EXPLICIT DELEGATION REQUEST: the user can name a sub-agent directly in their message — it appears as `@AgentName` or as a Markdown link `[@AgentName](codeg://agent/<agent_type>)`. Such a mention IS an explicit instruction to delegate the associated work to that agent, even when the user never names this tool. If the message names several agents, make one call per agent, each carrying that agent's slice of the work.

agent_type.description: Which local agent runs the sub-task. Pick the one best suited to the work — or, when the user's message names an agent via `@AgentName` / `codeg://agent/<agent_type>`, use that exact `<agent_type>` slug (e.g. `codeg://agent/claude_code` means `claude_code`).

task.description: The complete, self-contained prompt for the sub-agent. It has no access to this conversation or your context, so spell out everything: the goal, the relevant background and absolute file paths, any constraints, and exactly what to return.

working_dir.description: Absolute path the sub-agent runs in. Defaults to this session's working directory.

name: get_delegation_status
description: Collect delegated task results — or check on them — by the task_ids from delegate_to_agent. Pass a single id in the array to poll one task, or many at once to poll a whole fan-out in a single call. The response is ALWAYS a JSON object {"tasks":[...]} with one entry per id, in the order you asked — one entry for a single id, several for a fan-out; every entry carries that task's task_id and status, so you can always tell which task it is and where it stands. The wait_ms argument picks the mode: omit it for a non-blocking snapshot (poll), or pass wait_ms to wait — wait_ms>0 blocks up to that many ms (capped at 60000; re-call to keep waiting), wait_ms=0 blocks with no timeout for as long as the sub-agent runs. When polling several, the wait returns as soon as ANY requested task reaches a terminal state, so re-call to keep collecting the rest. When you just need the results, prefer blocking over repeated polling. Each task reports its current state — running, or a terminal completed / failed / canceled (or unknown if the id isn't recognized); a finished task includes its full result text. A wait ALSO returns early when a sub-agent becomes blocked on the user: that entry stays status "running" but carries blocked_on, meaning the sub-agent is parked on a permission / question / plan approval in Codeg and will not progress until a human answers. Tell the user about it — that is the one case where speaking up mid-wait is right — then wait again; each distinct prompt wakes the wait exactly once, so re-calling is safe and will not spin. While tasks are still running and you are simply waiting, do NOT emit any user-facing message between calls — just call again silently. Skip status narration like "still running", "not returned yet", or "continuing to wait"; it fragments the conversation. Speak to the user only when there is a terminal result to report, a task is blocked_on them, or something genuinely needs their input.

task_ids.description: One or more task_ids returned by delegate_to_agent — pass a single id to poll one task, or several to poll them together in one call. The response is always a JSON object {"tasks":[...]} with one entry per id (in this order) — one entry for a single id — and each entry carries that task's task_id and status. With wait_ms set, the call returns as soon as ANY of these tasks reaches a terminal state, or becomes blocked on you (status stays "running", plus a blocked_on field).

wait_ms.description: How long to wait. Omit for an immediate snapshot (poll). A positive value blocks up to that many milliseconds (capped at 60000). 0 means no timeout — block until a task reaches a terminal state, however long it takes. When several ids are given, the wait resolves as soon as ANY requested task becomes terminal, or as soon as one becomes blocked_on the user.

name: cancel_delegation
description: Stop a running delegated task by its task_id and tear down its sub-agent — use this only when you no longer want the result. Don't cancel just because a task is taking a while: substantial work can legitimately run for a long time, so prefer waiting on it (get_delegation_status with wait_ms) over canceling. If the task has already finished, nothing is canceled and its final result is returned instead.

name: check_user_feedback
description:
IMPORTANT: This tool gives you the ability to receive the user's real-time guidance while you work, preventing you from going down the wrong path and wasting effort. The user can type corrections, new requirements, or hints at any time during your turn — but you will NEVER see them unless you call this tool. Without it, you could spend minutes on work the user has already tried to redirect.

When to call:
- After thinking through your approach but BEFORE starting implementation — the user may have clarified requirements.
- Before making a significant decision (choosing an architecture, picking which files to modify, deciding on an approach) — the user may prefer a different direction.
- After completing a sub-task and before moving to the next step — the user may want to adjust priorities.
- When you pause to plan or organize your next steps — a natural checkpoint to read any pending guidance.

This is a quick, non-blocking snapshot that returns instantly. It either returns the user's messages (treat as HIGH-PRIORITY steering and adjust immediately) or an empty result (continue your current plan). Call it proactively — do not wait to be asked.

name: ask_user_question
description: Ask the user one or more multiple-choice questions and BLOCK until they answer. The questions render as interactive cards above the user's input box; this call returns only once the user submits their choices (or dismisses the card). Use ONLY when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make — one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults (e.g. which approach, which format, which library, which of several files). Do NOT use it to ask 'should I proceed?' or to confirm an obvious default, and do NOT use it for open-ended questions that aren't a small set of discrete choices. The user can always pick 'Other' and type a custom answer, so don't add your own 'Other' option. If you want to recommend a choice, put it first and append ' (Recommended)' to its label. Prefer ONE call with a few related questions over many sequential calls.

questions.description: 1-4 questions to ask in this single call.

question.description: The full question shown to the user.

header.description: Short category label (≤ 12 chars) shown as a chip, e.g. 'Approach', 'Format'.

multiSelect.description: If true, the user may select multiple options; otherwise it's a single choice.

label.description: Concise choice text. Append ' (Recommended)' to the first option to recommend it.

description.description: What this choice means or its trade-off.

name: get_session_info
description: Look up a session/conversation the user referenced in their message and return what it is: its title, which agent ran it, its status, workspace folder, git branch, model, message count, and token-usage stats — and, on request, a compact view of its most recent messages. RECOGNIZING A MENTIONED SESSION: the user can @-mention a past session directly in their message — it appears as a Markdown link `[Session title](codeg://session/<number>)`, whose text is that session's title and whose `<number>` is codeg's internal conversation id (e.g. `[Fix auth](codeg://session/214)` is the session titled 'Fix auth'). Such a mention IS the user explicitly pointing you at that session, even when they never name this tool — call it whenever what that session is about or what happened in it matters to the request (e.g. to continue its work, build on its results, answer questions about it, or summarize it). If the message mentions several sessions, make one call per session. Pass the NUMBER from the reference as `session_id` (it is codeg's internal conversation id, NOT the agent's own session id). The result is read-only and never modifies the session. A session that no longer exists returns a `found: false` result you can act on — it is not an error.

session_id.description: The number in the mentioned session's `codeg://session/<number>` link (codeg's internal conversation id). For example, given the mention `[Fix auth](codeg://session/214)`, pass 214.

max_messages.description: How many of the session's most recent turns to include as compact text. Defaults to 20; pass 0 for metadata only (faster, no transcript read). Capped at 200.

name: create_automation
description: Save a codeg Automation: a reusable job — a prompt plus a target project — that codeg runs on a cron schedule (or on demand) without anyone present. Use it when the user asks for work that should REPEAT or happen at a TIME rather than right now: 'every morning', 'each Monday', 'nightly', 'every 30 minutes', 'before standup', 'set up a recurring …'. Do NOT use it for work the user wants done in this conversation — just do that work. Each run starts a fresh headless session in its own worktree with no memory of this chat, so `prompt` must be completely self-contained: state the goal, the relevant paths, and what a finished run looks like. Creating an automation does not run it now; the tool returns the id and the next fire time so you can tell the user when it will first go off. The user can edit, disable, run, or delete it on the Automations page.

name.description: Short label shown in the automations list, e.g. 'Nightly dependency audit'.

prompt.description: The self-contained instruction each run executes. The run cannot see this conversation, so spell out the goal, the paths, and the definition of done.

cron.description: 5-field cron, and only 5 fields: `min hour day-of-month month day-of-week`, e.g. `0 9 * * 1-5` for weekdays at 09:00. Day-of-week is POSIX (0 and 7 are both Sunday). A seconds field is NOT supported and is rejected. Interpreted in `timezone`. OMIT this to create a manual automation the user runs on demand from the Automations page.

timezone.description: IANA zone the cron is read in, e.g. 'Asia/Shanghai'. Defaults to the machine's own zone — omit it unless the user names a different one.

action.description: What a fire does. 'launch_session' (default) runs the prompt immediately in a headless agent session. 'enqueue_task' instead drops a card on the user's to-dos for the board's queue to pick up — use it when the user wants scheduled work to land somewhere they review rather than run unattended.

agent_type.description: Which local agent runs it (e.g. 'claude_code', 'codex'). Defaults to the target project's configured agent — omit unless the user asks for a specific one.

folder_path.description: Absolute path of the target project. Defaults to the project this conversation is in; pass it only to target a different project already open in codeg.

enabled.description: Whether the schedule is live right away. Defaults to true; pass false to save it switched off.

name: create_work_task
description: Queue a card on codeg's to-dos. A task is a unit of work an agent later executes on its own branch/worktree, then hands back for the user to review and merge. Use it when the user wants work PARKED rather than done now — 'add a task to…', 'put this on the board', 'we should also fix X later' — or when you are splitting a large request into reviewable pieces and the user asked for that. Do NOT use it to do the thing the user just asked you to do in this conversation, and do NOT queue a task per trivial step. The executing agent starts cold with no view of this chat, so `prompt` must carry the full briefing. The tool returns the task id; the user tracks it in their to-dos.

title.description: Short card title, e.g. 'Migrate auth middleware to the new session API'.

prompt.description: The self-contained instruction the executing agent receives: the goal, the relevant files/paths, constraints, and what done looks like.

agent_type.description: Which local agent should run this task (e.g. 'claude_code', 'codex'). Omit to inherit the board's configured default.

folder_path.description: Absolute path of the target project. Defaults to the project this conversation is in; pass it only to target a different project already open in codeg.

name: task_progress
description: Report a short progress milestone for the work task you are executing. It shows up on the task's board card and timeline in real time, so the user can follow along without opening the session. Call it at meaningful checkpoints — finished exploring, tests passing, starting the refactor — not for every small step. Fire-and-forget: it never blocks your work and returns immediately.

message.description: One-line progress note, e.g. 'tests passing, starting cleanup'.

name: task_complete
description: Report the final outcome of the work task you are executing. Call it once, just before you end your reply. Pass verdict 'success' when the change is done and ready to review, 'needs_review' when it works but a human should double-check something specific (say what in the summary), or 'blocked' when you could not complete the task (the summary must say why). The task settles when your turn ends: success and needs_review send it to review, blocked marks it failed. If you never call this tool the task still settles normally from your turn's end.

verdict.description: How the task ended from your point of view.

summary.description: Short result summary shown on the task card: what changed, and anything the reviewer should look at.
